# **Next-Generation Radar Fire Control Systems: A Comparative Analysis of Conventional Tracking Architectures and PMCW DCM MIMO Radar-on-Chip Solutions**

The architecture of defense sensing and engagement is undergoing a profound paradigm shift. The historical reliance on massive, mechanically steered analog radar platforms is rapidly giving way to highly integrated, software-defined, and cognitively adaptive digital sensors. At the core of this transition is the evolution of the fire control radar (FCR), a highly specialized class of sensor engineered specifically to determine the precise spatial coordinates and kinematic trajectory of an aerial, surface, or ground target to direct kinetic effectors.1 Unlike volumetric search radars, which are optimized for broad spatial coverage and early warning, fire control radars are characterized by highly concentrated beamwidths, elevated pulse repetition frequencies (PRF), and exceedingly short pulse widths.2 While many legacy systems incorporate target illumination modules for semi-active missile guidance, the scope of this extensive analysis is strictly confined to the continuous detection, precise ranging, and algorithmic tracking functions.1

As modern battlefields become increasingly populated by asymmetric threats—such as low radar cross-section (RCS) unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and highly maneuverable drone swarms—the demand for highly precise, battery-operable fire control sensors at the tactical edge has surged exponentially.4 This demand has catalyzed the development of advanced algorithms, including Interacting Multiple Model (IMM) tracking, cognitive waveform optimization, and deep learning-based target classification.6 Concurrently, the semiconductor industry has introduced Phase-Modulated Continuous Wave (PMCW) Digital Code Modulation (DCM) Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) Radar-on-Chip (RoC) architectures.8 These ultra-compact, silicon-based platforms synthesize massive virtual apertures, fundamentally resolving the interference and resolution limitations of legacy Frequency-Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) systems. This report provides an exhaustive technical evaluation of traditional and cognitive fire control tracking methodologies, rigorously contrasting them with the capabilities of PMCW DCM MIMO RoC platforms, while defining the critical engineering strategies required to balance high-fidelity target processing with the stringent power constraints of battery-operated edge systems.

## **The Fundamentals of Fire Control Detection and Tracking**

The operational lifecycle of a fire control radar is strictly segmented into three sequential phases, dictated by the physical limitations of its highly directive "pencil beam" radiation pattern. Because an FCR focuses its radio frequency (RF) energy to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on a single point in space, it lacks the beam width required to efficiently search large volumes of the sky.2

The first phase is designation, often referred to as vectoring. During this phase, a secondary surveillance radar or an external tactical control network provides the FCR with the approximate spatial coordinates of the incoming threat.1 Once cued to the general vicinity of the target, the radar initiates the acquisition phase. The FCR executes a localized, prearranged search pattern—such as a raster scan, spiral scan, or nodding scan—within a confined spatial volume until the target echo exceeds the established constant false alarm rate (CFAR) detection threshold.1

Upon successful detection, the system transitions into the track phase, wherein the radar establishes a closed-loop tracking sequence, actively following the target's kinematics. Tracking paradigms generally fall into two categories: Track-While-Scan (TWS) and Continuous Track.2 In TWS, the radar maintains a sector scan, establishing and updating multiple target tracks simultaneously by correlating sequential plot detections over multiple scans. Conversely, Continuous Track dedicates the entire resource budget of the radar to a single target, providing a continuous, high-update-rate stream of kinematic data.1 Traditional continuous trackers operate with exceptionally high PRFs and narrow pulse widths to achieve extreme range and velocity resolution, though this limits the maximum unambiguous range and introduces complexities in initial detection.2

![][image1]

### **Ranging, Angular Estimation, and Monopulse Architectures**

Accurate spatial localization for fire control requires both precise ranging (derived from the time delay of the returning pulse) and angular estimation (azimuth and elevation). Historically, continuous trackers utilized conical scanning, a mechanical technique where the radar beam is rapidly rotated around a central boresight axis.2 By analyzing the amplitude modulation of the returning target echoes as the beam sweeps across the target, the system derives an angular error signal to mechanically drive the antenna servos and keep the target centered.11 However, conical scanning is critically flawed in the presence of amplitude scintillation. Target RCS fluctuates wildly from pulse to pulse due to minor aspect changes, structural vibrations, or rotating components (such as propeller blades or turbine fans).10 These target-induced amplitude fluctuations corrupt the scanning error signal, causing the track to wander or break lock completely.

To circumvent the vulnerabilities of sequential amplitude measurement, modern fire control systems utilize monopulse radar architectures. Monopulse systems derive a complete angular error vector from a single transmitted pulse by receiving the echo through multiple, physically offset antenna feeds or sub-arrays.2 By comparing the amplitude (Amplitude Comparison Monopulse) or the phase (Phase Comparison Monopulse) of the returning signal across these simultaneous, overlapping channels, the radar generates an instantaneous tracking error signal.14

Because the angular data is extracted simultaneously from a single pulse, any pulse-to-pulse amplitude fluctuations of the target are entirely canceled out through the algorithmic ratio of the sum and difference channels.12 The sum channel is utilized for target detection and range determination, while the difference channels provide the angular deviation.11 Monopulse techniques exhibit exceptional precision, frequently resolving target angles to a fraction of the antenna's physical beamwidth, making them indispensable for precision guided munition tracking.16 However, the fundamental limitation of analog monopulse tracking is its susceptibility to multi-target interference. When two or more targets occupy the exact same range and Doppler resolution cell, their complex amplitudes interfere. The monopulse ratio becomes distorted, causing the calculated angle to wander wildly between the targets—a phenomenon known as glint—resulting in massive angular estimation errors.15

### **Algorithmic Tracking and Plot Association**

Raw radar detections, referred to as plots, represent instantaneous snapshots of energy exceeding the CFAR threshold. These unassociated plots must be subjected to intensive algorithmic processing to form stable, predictive tracks. The tracking architecture executes four primary functions: plot-to-track association, track smoothing, track initiation, and track maintenance.18

In benign environments, simple Nearest Neighbor algorithms suffice for associating a new plot with an existing track. However, in dense clutter environments or when tracking multiple closely spaced targets, these simplistic algorithms fail. Modern fire control computers therefore employ Probabilistic Data Association (PDA) algorithms.18 PDA does not force a hard decision to associate a single plot with a track; rather, it calculates the statistical probability of all validated measurements within a predicted tracking gate originating from the true target. The state estimate is then updated using a probabilistically weighted sum of all valid hypotheses, significantly improving track continuity in heavy clutter.18

For highly maneuvering targets, the underlying mathematical model of the tracking filter becomes the limiting factor. Standard Kalman filters are typically initialized with a Constant Velocity (CV) or Constant Acceleration (CA) model.6 If a target executes a high-G evasive maneuver, these rigid models experience severe lag, causing the tracking gate to decouple from the actual target position, leading to track divergence. To mitigate this, advanced tracking networks deploy Interacting Multiple Model (IMM) estimators.20

The IMM algorithm functions within a Bayesian framework, simultaneously processing multiple dynamic kinematic models in parallel Kalman filters.21 A typical IMM configuration might include a CV model with low process noise for cruising flight, a CV model with high process noise for erratic movement, a Coordinated Turn (CT) model for banking, and a move-stop-move model for hovering UAVs.20 A Markov chain transition matrix dictates the statistical probability of the target switching between these kinematic states.20 During each radar scan, the IMM estimator calculates the likelihood of each model based on the residual errors of the respective Kalman filters. The final state estimate and error covariance matrix are calculated as a probabilistically weighted combination of all individual filter outputs.22 This interactive mixing allows the fire control radar to instantaneously adapt its predictive gate to abrupt evasive maneuvers without losing track continuity.19

## **Advanced Fire Control Methodologies: Cognitive Radar and Artificial Intelligence**

While IMM filters and PDA algorithms heavily optimize the receiver's data processing backend, the transmission parameters of traditional fire control radars remain relatively rigid. The evolution toward Cognitive Radar (CR) transforms the sensor into an intelligent, closed-loop system capable of perceiving its electromagnetic environment, learning from past interactions, and dynamically redesigning its transmitted waveforms in real-time to optimize tracking performance.7

### **Cognitive Waveform Optimization**

In a fully cognitive fire control architecture, the radar continuously updates its broadcast waveform parameters to minimize target state estimation errors and maximize the probability of detection (![][image2]).7 This dynamic adaptation is frequently modeled mathematically as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), where the radar takes "actions"—such as altering pulse width, PRF, or frequency modulation slope—to maximize an information-theoretic reward based on the target's current state.26

Advanced optimization frameworks, such as Entropy Reward Q-Learning (ERQL) and Criterion-Based Optimization (CBO), are utilized to autonomously select the optimal waveform from a predetermined library.7 For instance, if the IMM estimator detects a target entering a highly maneuverable state (e.g., transitioning from a CV model to a CT model), the cognitive radar loop will dynamically decrease the pulse duration to improve range resolution and increase the frequency modulation slope to enhance Doppler resolution. Numerical results indicate that ERQL and CBO methods significantly reduce the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of both target position and velocity tracking compared to fixed-parameter transmission approaches.7

In complex multi-target scenarios, cognitive MIMO radars utilize sophisticated power allocation strategies. Instead of uniformly broadcasting energy, the system solves a constrained optimization problem to maximize Mutual Information (MI).25 Utilizing water-filling algorithms, the cognitive radar selectively concentrates its transmit power into specific frequency bins or spatial sectors where the target's Extended Target Impulse Response (TIR) scattering is strongest, or conversely, reallocates power to enhance the detectability of distant, low-SNR targets while starving power from sectors with known high-SNR tracks.27 This adaptive waveform synthesis ensures that the radar maintains optimal performance even under stringent energy constraints.

| Cognitive Optimization Technique | Primary Function | Application in Fire Control |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Entropy Reward Q-Learning (ERQL)** | Machine learning framework for waveform selection | Autonomously adjusts PRF and pulse width based on target maneuvering state to minimize RMSE.7 |
| **Criterion-Based Optimization (CBO)** | Real-time parameter matching | Merges radar and target into a closed loop, updating broadcasts based on kinematic models.7 |
| **Water-Filling Power Allocation** | Frequency-domain energy distribution | Concentrates transmit power into frequency bins with significant target scattering, maximizing Mutual Information (MI).29 |
| **Adaptive Gradient Descent Genetic Algorithm (GD-AGA)** | Time-domain waveform approximation | Minimizes Energy Spectral Density (ESD) loss and Peak-to-Average Power Ratio (PAPR) for MIMO transmission.30 |

### **Deep Learning and Multiple Hypothesis Tracking**

The integration of deep learning neural networks with conventional statistical filters has given rise to highly robust hybrid cognitive architectures.6 Artificial intelligence models such as YOLO (You Only Look Once) and Mask R-CNN are deployed directly within the signal processing pipeline to perform rapid target classification based on micro-Doppler signatures and Radar Cross Section (RCS) analysis.6 Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks are fused with Extended Kalman Filters (EKF) to refine nonlinear trajectory predictions, recognizing complex, erratic kinematic patterns that purely mathematical Markov models fail to capture.6 Simulation data indicates that combining conventional filtering with AI models can increase detection accuracy to 99.8% while drastically reducing false positive rates.6

Furthermore, to combat dense environmental clutter, severe multipath fading, and electronic countermeasures, algorithms like Multiple Hypothesis Tracking (MHT) are integrated into Rao-Blackwellized Particle Filters (RBPF).31 Unlike standard PDA, which collapses all hypotheses into a single updated state vector at each time step, MHT maintains a branching tree of possible track associations over time.18 By delaying hard association decisions until future radar scans provide sufficient statistical confidence, the algorithm can accurately prune false tracks generated by clutter or jamming.31 This allows advanced fire control systems to maintain a continuous lock on low-altitude, highly maneuverable drones navigating through heavy urban environments.31

### **Electronic Protection and LPI Waveforms**

In modern contested electromagnetic environments, radar survivability is strictly dependent on Low Probability of Intercept (LPI) characteristics. A fire control radar that emits massive spikes of energy is immediately targeted by enemy Electronic Support (ES) receivers and Anti-Radiation Missiles (ARM).32 Cognitive radars actively design transmit waveforms that are deliberately mismatched to the tuning parameters of hostile intercept receivers.32

By utilizing spread-spectrum techniques, ultra-wideband frequency hopping, and low peak-power noise-like modulations (such as pseudo-random bit patterns), the radar achieves a massive processing gain internally through pulse compression, while appearing merely as ambient background thermal noise to adversarial interceptors.32 Advanced AI-driven controllers continuously analyze the spectrum to align mutual interference and allocate resources, dynamically hopping frequencies to ensure the fire control lock-on sequence remains completely undetected by legacy electronic warfare suites.23

## **PMCW DCM MIMO Radar-on-Chip (RoC) Architecture**

To execute the immense computational load required by cognitive algorithms, MHT, and complex waveform generation, while simultaneously adhering to the severe Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWaP-C) constraints of tactical edge devices, the industry has pivoted toward highly integrated millimeter-wave (mmWave) Radar-on-Chip (RoC) solutions. Traditional automotive and short-range tracking radars have heavily relied on Frequency-Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) designs.8 While FMCW boasts low implementation complexity and low power consumption, it suffers from several critical physical limitations that render it unsuitable for advanced fire control.

FMCW systems exhibit inherent range-Doppler coupling. Because range is calculated via a frequency shift, a highly maneuverable target experiencing a rapid Doppler shift introduces a simultaneous artificial shift in the calculated range, inducing systemic tracking errors.8 Furthermore, FMCW radars have a strictly limited maximum unambiguous velocity when utilizing Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM) MIMO setups, and they suffer from high-range sidelobes that drastically reduce High-Contrast Resolution (HCR).8

To permanently resolve these bottlenecks, the Phase-Modulated Continuous Wave (PMCW) architecture utilizing Digital Code Modulation (DCM) has emerged as a technologically superior alternative.8 Platforms such as the Uhnder S80 and S81 RoCs exemplify the bleeding edge of this technology, operating in the 76–81 GHz band and providing unprecedented levels of integration.9

### **Digital Code Modulation and PMCW Mechanics**

Unlike FMCW, which transmits a linear frequency sweep (chirp), PMCW radar transmits a continuous carrier wave that is phase-modulated—typically utilizing binary phase-shift keying (BPSK)—by a high-speed pseudo-random digital code.38 The range resolution of a PMCW system is fundamentally dictated by the chip rate (the duration of a single phase state), while the maximum unambiguous range is determined by the total temporal length of the code sequence.8 Because range and velocity are processed in entirely separate domains, PMCW completely eliminates the range-Doppler coupling inherent to FMCW systems, providing pristine kinematic measurements for fire control computers.8

At the receiver architecture, the returning echo is digitized by high-speed Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs) and passed into a massive bank of digital correlators. The receiver performs pulse compression by correlating the incoming signal against the known transmitted code.38 To maximize detection performance, systems employ specific mathematical sequences, such as Almost Perfect Autocorrelation Sequences (APAS) or complementary Golay sequences.38 The autocorrelation of these specific codes yields an ideal "thumbtack-like" ambiguity function—a sharp, distinct correlation peak at the exact target range and virtually zero correlation elsewhere.8

### **Virtual Aperture Synthesis via Code-Domain MIMO**

The true disruptive power of PMCW DCM lies in its native support for massive MIMO configurations. In a conventional phased array fire control radar, angular resolution is physically constrained by the total aperture size and the number of physical transceiver modules. To increase resolution, the physical dish must be enlarged. MIMO radar circumvents this physical limitation by transmitting mathematically orthogonal waveforms simultaneously from ![][image3] transmit antennas.38

When these overlapping orthogonal echoes are captured by ![][image4] receive antennas, the digital back-end utilizes matched filters to separate the codes, mathematically synthesizing a virtual antenna array consisting of ![][image5] independent spatial elements.39 This massive virtual aperture allows the system to achieve the high-resolution performance of a massive antenna array without the associated physical hardware complexity, weight, or power consumption.39

To ensure perfect orthogonality and zero cross-talk between the simultaneously broadcasting transmitters, code-domain MIMO techniques are employed. For example, outer Hadamard coding can be overlaid onto the base APAS sequences, utilizing the optimal cross-correlation properties of Hadamard matrices to isolate each transmit channel at the receiver.38

The Uhnder S80 RoC represents a pinnacle of this architecture, integrating 12 transmit channels and 16 receive channels directly onto the silicon.9 By applying DCM MIMO techniques, the S80 synthesizes an astounding 192 Virtual Receive Channels (VRx) on a single 12.8 mm x 8.21 mm chip package.9 For mass-market or highly constrained applications, the Uhnder S81 offers a scaled-down 12 Tx by 8 Rx configuration, yielding 96 VRx.37 The S80 architecture supports multichip cascading, allowing up to four RoCs to be linked, generating an unprecedented 3072 VRx with full MIMO scaling, effectively miniaturizing a massive AESA radar into a modular, board-level component.9

### **Computational Pipeline and Baseband Processing**

Translating up to 192 channels of gigahertz-bandwidth RF data into a cohesive 4D point cloud (encompassing Range, Velocity, Azimuth, and Elevation) requires immense computational throughput. Traditional MIMO architectures offload raw ADC data to external FPGA or CPU clusters via high-speed links, incurring unacceptable latency and power draw that violate the strict timing requirements of closed-loop fire control.21

The S80 and S81 RoCs resolve this bottleneck by placing the processing directly on the silicon die. The architecture utilizes dual ARM Cortex-R5F CPUs running at 667 MHz for high-level system management, algorithmic execution, and API interfacing.47 To handle the massive parallel mathematical workload, the chips integrate dual Tensilica-P5 Digital Signal Processors (DSPs) clocked at 533 MHz.47 These dedicated DSPs are optimized to accelerate heavy matrix math, pulse compression, complex multidimensional FFTs, and correlation algorithms.47 This highly integrated, software-defined hardware pipeline is capable of up to 20 Tera-Ops of baseband processing, delivering simultaneous multidimensional measurements with virtually zero latency.9 A dedicated ARM Cortex M0+ operates as the Chip Control Processor and Functional Safety Manager, executing in a lockstep configuration with a Hardware Security Module (HSM) to ensure AEC-Q104 and ASIL-B compliance, protecting the sensor against adversarial cyber-intrusion and spoofing.44

## **Comparative Analysis: Traditional FCR vs. PMCW DCM MIMO RoC**

When evaluating highly integrated PMCW DCM MIMO RoC technology against traditional fire control systems, several profound operational advantages emerge, particularly regarding angular precision, target discrimination, and electronic protection.

### **Angular Accuracy and Sub-Resolution Estimation**

Traditional fire control radars achieve extreme angular tracking accuracy primarily through massive physical antenna apertures and phase-comparison monopulse techniques. By measuring the phase gradient across a large physical antenna face, monopulse radars can isolate a single target with milliradian accuracy, providing the precise data required for ballistic calculation.15 However, as previously noted, analog monopulse logic inherently assumes that only one dominant scatterer exists within a specific range-Doppler cell. If a swarm of micro-drones flies in close formation, the monopulse error signal merges the phase centers of the individual targets, resulting in glint and a wandering track centroid that fails entirely to resolve individual threats.15

Conversely, PMCW MIMO RoCs rely on the mathematical synthesis of a massive virtual aperture. While the physical aperture of an RoC is restricted by the small form factor of the chip and its associated PCB antenna layout, the creation of 192 virtual receivers provides sufficient spatial sampling to utilize advanced Digital Beamforming (DBF) algorithms.4 By applying high-resolution subspace algorithms—such as the Multiple Signal Classification (MUSIC) algorithm or Estimation of Signal Parameters via Rotational Invariance Techniques (ESPRIT)—to the massive MIMO covariance matrix, the radar achieves sub-resolution angular accuracy.50 ESPRIT, in particular, offers superior resolution for multi-target scenarios with reduced computational complexity.50 This mathematical super-resolution enables the RoC to distinctly resolve, classify, and track multiple tightly spaced targets within the exact same range and velocity bin, effectively nullifying the glint vulnerabilities that cripple legacy analog fire control trackers.40

### **High Contrast Resolution (HCR) and Clutter Rejection**

A critical performance metric for modern edge tracking is High Contrast Resolution (HCR). HCR defines the radar's ability to detect an object with an extremely low RCS (e.g., a carbon-fiber drone, a pedestrian, or a stealth cruise missile) located in immediate physical proximity to an object with a massive RCS (e.g., an armored vehicle, a truck, or a building).8 Traditional FMCW radars utilize FFTs for range processing, which mathematically results in a broad ![][image7]\-function response. The high-range sidelobes emanating from the massive target's ![][image7] response inevitably bury the primary peak of the small target, rendering the low-RCS threat completely invisible to the tracking filter.8

PMCW DCM inherently eliminates this critical blind spot. Because the correlation of the transmitted APAS codes generates a pristine thumbtack-like ambiguity response, the signal drop-off around a detected target is exceptionally sharp. Laboratory analyses of binary-phase radar demonstrate sidelobe suppression exceeding 35 dB.8 This phenomenal High Contrast Resolution allows the fire control logic to maintain an uninterrupted lock on a micro-drone even as it hovers directly alongside a massive, highly radar-reflective structure.8

### **Interference Resilience and Electronic Protection**

Traditional fire control radars operating in highly congested and contested environments must contend with both adversarial electronic attack (jamming) and unintentional mutual interference from friendly radar systems operating nearby. PMCW DCM architecture is natively robust against both spoofing and cross-interference. The Interference Susceptibility Factor (ISF) is significantly lower and far more predictable for PMCW compared to FMCW.8

In a dense electromagnetic environment, FMCW chirps crossing paths create severe broadband noise spikes. The interference spectral density factor (the ![][image8]\-factor) for misaligned FMCW radars can reach up to 10, resulting in interference with ten times the power spectral density, effectively blinding the victim radar.8 In contrast, the ![][image8]\-factor for PMCW is generally equal to unity, indicating highly manageable interference.8 Because the DCM system relies on specific, cryptographically secure pseudo-random code sequences (bearing similarities to CDMA military communications technology), any incoming RF signal that does not perfectly match the exact expected local code sequence is mathematically filtered out as low-level background noise during the correlation process.8 This inherently prevents adversarial spoofing attacks, as the adversary cannot predict or replicate the instantaneous, randomized digital code required to inject a coherent false target into the radar's tracking filter.37

## **Power Optimization Strategies for Battery-Operated Radar on Chip**

While the processing throughput required to decode up to 192 channels of gigahertz-rate PMCW data is immense, deploying these advanced RoCs in portable, battery-operated platforms—such as dismounted infantry fire control sights, autonomous UGV sentries, or drone-mounted C-UAS tracking modules—demands aggressive and innovative power optimization.53 A highly capable MIMO RoC like the Uhnder S80 consumes approximately 9 to 9.5 Watts during standard active operation.9 Managing this thermal and power load on a constrained, non-rechargeable battery supply necessitates a multi-layered optimization strategy bridging hardware design, firmware management, and advanced signal processing.

### **Duty Cycle Configurations and Dynamic Power Gating**

The most direct and effective method to prolong battery endurance in an RoC is aggressive dynamic duty cycling.9 The baseline 9.5 W consumption rating of the S80 is measured at a continuous 50% duty cycle.9 By dynamically altering the frame repetition rate and scan integration times via the software-defined APIs, the radar can heavily throttle its power draw based on the immediate tactical context.9

Advanced power management integrated circuits (PMICs) and embedded microcontrollers orchestrate complex deep sleep states.47 Techniques such as power gating entirely shut off supply voltage to unutilized RF transceiver blocks and DSP cores when no active target is within the tracking gate.57 Clock gating halts the high-frequency oscillator signals to digital circuits when idle, preventing dynamic power dissipation. If the system is operating in a passive early-warning or broad-search mode, the radar can operate at a highly reduced duty cycle, consuming minimal milliwatts.56 Upon detecting a kinetic threat that breaches the CFAR threshold, the system instantaneously wakes the dormant Tx/Rx channels and Tensilica DSPs, ramping up to a high-duty-cycle continuous track to provide the 50+ frames per second update rate required for high-fidelity fire control.57

![][image9]

### **Computational Offloading and Algorithmic Efficiency**

To minimize the absolute energy expended during the active duty cycle, the computational complexity of the signal processing algorithms must be aggressively streamlined. The generation of a 4D radar data cube requires highly intensive multidimensional FFTs across range, Doppler, azimuth, and elevation dimensions.48

Optimized RoC architectures employ dedicated hardware accelerators specifically designed to handle massive matrix operations with extreme energy efficiency, offloading these tasks from the general-purpose ARM CPUs.48 Furthermore, algorithmic innovations such as the Subaperture-Recursive (SAR) SPICE method enable the recursive refinement of target location parameters without requiring the massive, high-dimensional matrix inversions demanded by traditional super-resolution algorithms.4 By updating the state recursively with each new block of received data, the SAR-SPICE method drastically cuts memory access operations and logic toggling within the DSP, directly translating to measurable battery savings.4 Systems utilizing Energy Harvester (EH) chips paired with Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) algorithms further optimize this power delivery, ensuring stable operation even under fluctuating ambient energy conditions.59

### **Networked Energy Saving via Peer-to-Peer Sensor Fusion**

In distributed defense environments, individual battery-operated radar nodes do not need to process tracking data in strict isolation. Novel lightweight peer-to-peer energy-saving methodologies allow physically adjacent sensors to cooperate, sharing the tracking burden.60 Using localized, low-power communication protocols (such as Bluetooth Low Energy or Sub-1 GHz RF links), a cluster of battery-powered radar nodes can dynamically elect a "leader" node based on current battery reserves and optimal target geometry.60

The elected leader node activates its high-power DSPs and dense MIMO array to maintain the continuous track, transmitting the refined coordinates to the central fire control network. Meanwhile, the subordinate nodes remain in a passive, low-power listening state or power down entirely.60 Experimental evaluations of these cooperative tracker networks demonstrate that shifting from independent tracking to dynamic peer-to-peer delegation can reduce the average energy consumption per location report by up to 240% per node, fundamentally extending the operational endurance of the distributed tactical sensor grid.60

### **Cognitive Power Allocation**

Expanding the POMDP framework of cognitive radar to encompass the physical battery state introduces the concept of power-aware target tracking.27 Rather than transmitting orthogonal waveforms with uniform power allocation across all physical antennas, the cognitive RoC utilizes the expected target range and predicted angular position derived from the IMM filter to solve a constrained optimization problem.23

If the cognitive engine determines that a target is at a close range with a high SNR, it intelligently reduces the transmit energy allocated to the specific physical antennas steering toward that spatial sector.27 Conversely, it reallocates that conserved power to enhance the detectability of distant, low-RCS targets, or simply banks the energy to extend overall battery life. By continuously monitoring the mutual information gain relative to the joules expended, the cognitive PMCW RoC transcends static hardware efficiency, achieving software-defined, mission-adaptive energy sustainability.27

## **Conclusion**

The architecture of fire control systems is undergoing a rapid, software-defined evolution, moving away from systems constrained by physical mechanics toward intelligent, silicon-based networks. Traditional track-while-scan and continuous tracking paradigms, once reliant on mechanically vulnerable hardware, interference-prone FMCW analog processing, and rigid Kalman filtering, are being systematically replaced by highly integrated, cognitive digital architectures.

The advent of the Phase-Modulated Continuous Wave Digital Code Modulation MIMO Radar-on-Chip fundamentally resolves historical tracking limitations. By leveraging computationally intensive digital code correlation and massive virtual aperture synthesis, PMCW architectures effectively eliminate range-Doppler coupling, bypass the glint vulnerabilities inherent to analog monopulse systems, and provide unprecedented High Contrast Resolution necessary to separate micro-threats from heavy background clutter. Furthermore, the cryptographic nature of the binary phase sequences inherently provides advanced Low Probability of Intercept capabilities and robust immunity against adversarial spoofing and dense mutual interference.

Crucially, the successful deployment of these 20-Tera-Op processing engines to the tactical edge relies on aggressive SWaP-C optimization. Through millisecond-level dynamic power gating, the utilization of highly efficient Tensilica DSP cores, and cognitive, power-aware waveform allocation, battery-operated RoC modules can sustain high-fidelity, 4D tracking grids without tethering to massive external power generators. As artificial intelligence models like deep neural networks and Interacting Multiple Model filters continue to seamlessly merge with programmable RF front-ends, the resulting cognitive fire control sensors will provide unparalleled target discrimination, energy efficiency, and kinetic accuracy in the most contested and resource-constrained environments of the modern era.
